urgent.heading: Urgent — use EpiPen now
urgent.primary_message: Use the adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) immediately into the outer thigh. Then call 10177.
red_flags: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat
Difficulty breathing, wheezing, or a tight throat
Sudden hives or red welts spreading over the body
Vomiting, severe stomach cramps, or sudden diarrhoea

what_is_it.heading: Anaphylaxis in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction that can be fatal within minutes if untreated.
paragraphs: It happens when the immune system massively overreacts to something usually harmless — a food, a sting, a medicine, or latex. Blood vessels leak, airways swell, blood pressure drops.

Adrenaline (epinephrine) is the only first-line treatment. An auto-injector like an EpiPen delivers it into the thigh muscle. Antihistamines and inhalers are not a substitute. After using an EpiPen, the person still needs hospital care because symptoms can return hours later.

items.headline: Minutes
items.body: Severe anaphylaxis can be fatal within 15 minutes. Speed of treatment is everything.

items.headline: Top triggers
items.body: Peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, eggs, bee or wasp stings, medicines (often antibiotics), and latex.

items.headline: Second wave
items.body: Up to 1 in 5 people have a second reaction 4–12 hours later, even after improving. Hospital observation is essential.

items.headline: EpiPen first
items.body: Adrenaline auto-injector is the only first-line treatment. It is safe to use — withholding it is what causes harm.

pull_quote.text: If you are not sure whether it is anaphylaxis — use the EpiPen anyway. The risk of using it unnecessarily is small. The risk of not using it can be fatal.

signs.heading: What you might see
signs.lede: Anaphylaxis usually starts within minutes of exposure. Symptoms involve more than one body system — skin, breathing, circulation, or gut.

items.title: Skin
items.description: Hives or red welts, intense itching, flushing, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or eyes.

items.title: Breathing
items.description: Wheezing, tight throat, hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, persistent cough, struggling to breathe.

items.title: Circulation
items.description: Rapid pulse, low blood pressure, dizziness, fainting, pale or clammy skin, collapse.

items.title: Gut and general
items.description: Stomach cramps, vomiting, sudden diarrhoea. A feeling of doom is a recognised warning sign.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Antihistamines are enough to stop anaphylaxis.
items.fact: Antihistamines treat mild allergy symptoms. They cannot reverse anaphylaxis. Adrenaline is the only first-line treatment.

items.myth: I should wait and see if it gets worse before using the EpiPen.
items.fact: Use it as soon as anaphylaxis is suspected. Delay is the most common cause of death. Adrenaline is safe — withholding it is dangerous.

items.myth: If they feel better after the EpiPen, they don't need to go to hospital.
items.fact: They still need hospital observation. Symptoms can return hours later (biphasic reaction). A second EpiPen may be needed.

items.myth: You only need an EpiPen if you have had a severe reaction before.
items.fact: A first severe reaction can come without warning, especially in people with known food or insect allergies. Talk to a doctor about getting an EpiPen.

action_steps.heading: What to do — minute by minute

items.title: Use the EpiPen into the outer thigh
items.description: Through clothes is fine. Hold firmly for 10 seconds. Note the time you used it.

items.title: Call 10177 or 112 immediately
items.description: Say 'anaphylaxis'. Even if the person seems better, they need hospital observation.

items.title: Lay them flat, raise their legs
items.description: Helps blood pressure. If they are vomiting, lay them on their side. If breathing is hard, let them sit up — never standing.

items.title: Second EpiPen if no improvement in 5 minutes
items.description: Give a second dose into the other thigh. Most EpiPens come in a 2-pack for this reason.

items.title: Stay with them until paramedics arrive
items.description: Watch breathing and pulse. Be ready to perform CPR. Give the used EpiPen to the paramedics.

get_help.heading: Who to call right now
get_help.lede: Anaphylaxis is always an emergency, even if symptoms ease after the EpiPen. Get the person to hospital.
